findings.title: Calling get_memory_info() across all shard buffers redundantly queries every Redis cluster node per process
findings.body: In `SpanFlusher.submit`, the code iterates over `self.buffers.values()` and calls `buffer.get_memory_info()` on each `SpansBuffer` instance (lines 300-303). Unlike `record_stored_segments()` which is scoped to `assigned_shards`, `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` queries `iter_Hosts()` across the entire Redis cluster (`self.client`), not just the shards assigned to that buffer. When `num_processes > 1`, calling `get_memory_info()` on every buffer in `self.buffers` performs `num_processes` times as many `INFO MEMORY` network calls to Redis on every batch submission, adding unnecessary latency and load to Redis. Calling `get_memory_info()` on a single buffer instance (or keeping `self.buffer`) is sufficient and avoids the N-fold duplication.

findings.title: join() fails to terminate remaining flusher processes if deadline expires mid-loop
findings.body: In `SpanFlusher.join()`, the loop over `self.processes.items()` checks if `remaining_time <= 0` and executes `break` (lines 338-341) before reaching `process.terminate()` (lines 346-347). If a timeout is provided and the first process takes until the deadline to exit (or `next_step.join(timeout)` consumes the entire timeout), the loop breaks early and never calls `process.terminate()` on any of the subsequent flusher processes, leaving them running in the background after `join()` returns.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag name 'shards' vs 'shard' and potential high tag cardinality
findings.body: In `SpanFlusher.main`, `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` (line 185) and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` (line 195) use the tag key `"shard": shard_tag`, whereas `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` (line 199) uses the plural key `"shards": shard_tag`. In addition to the inconsistent tag naming across sibling metrics, when a process handles multiple shards (e.g. with the default `--flusher-processes=1`), `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list of all assigned partition indices (such as `"0,1,2,3,..."`), which changes across consumer rebalances and can create high-cardinality metric tags.
